--- format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: "Lecture 2 -- Refresher of basic statistical models" slide-number: true toc: false margin: 0.1 auto-stretch: false fig-width: 7 fig-height: 7 lang: en --- # Overview section {visibility="hidden"} ## {.center content-align="center"}
::: {.center style="font-size: 140%;"} **Statistical modeling basics** :::
![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/slr-viz-1.png){width="40%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Simple linear regression"}
::: {style="font-size: 90%;"} WILD(FISH) 8390 :::
# Linear models {visibility="hidden"} ## Today's Topics - Linear models * Classical * Bayesian
- Generalized linear models * Classical * Bayesian ## Linear models {style="font-size: 90%;"} All ANOVAs and fixed-effects regression models are linear models.
You must understand linear models before you can apply more advanced models such as GLMs, GAMS, hierarchical models etc...
![](figure/Rencher_Schaal_book.jpg){height="300"} ![](figure/Hocking_book.jpg){height="300"}
## Simple linear regression {.smaller} Simple linear regression is the most basic linear model. $$ \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i \qquad \qquad y_i \sim \mathrm{Norm}(\mu_i, \sigma^2) $$ ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fragment} $y$ is variously called: - response variable - outcome variable - dependent variable ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fragment} It's worse for $x$ - predictor variable - explanatory variable - independent variable - covariate, exposure, etc... ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} We observe $x$ and $y$. The expected value of $y_i$ is $\mu_i$.\ We'd like to estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, called the "coefficients".\ A residual is $\varepsilon_i=y_i-\mu_i$. $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the residuals. ::: ## Simple linear regression example Suppose your data look like this: ::: {style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} width <- c(0.30, 0.91, 0.89, 0.24, 0.77, 0.56, 0.59, 0.92, 0.81, 0.59) ## x mass <- c(0.08, 0.59, 0.18, 0.17, 0.42, 0.71, 0.49, 0.75, 0.46, 0.04) ## y ``` ::: ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/slr-viz-1.png){width=4in} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.fragment}
Classical inference is easy: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = mass ~ width) Coefficients: (Intercept) width 0.02742 0.54951 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Bayesian inference with JAGS {style="font-size: 90%;"} We will use JAGS and the R packages 'rjags' and 'jagsUI'. JAGS can be downloaded [here](https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/).
The basic steps of Bayesian analysis with JAGS are: 1. Write a model in the BUGS language in a text file 2. Put data in a named list 3. Create a function to generate random initial values 4. Specify the parameters you want to monitor 5. Use MCMC to draw posterior samples 6. Use posterior samples for inference and prediction ## Bayesian linear regression -- JAGS model {style="font-size: 90%;"} The model is in a text file named `lm.jag`\ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model { # Priors ## dnorm arguments: mean and precision (1/variance) beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1) ## Prior on intercept beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1) ## Prior on slope sigmaSq ~ dunif(0, 2) ## Prior on residual variance # Model for the data for(i in 1:n) { mu[i] <- beta0 + beta1*x[i] y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], 1/sigmaSq) } } ``` ::: ## Bayesian linear regression -- data, inits, etc {style="font-size: 80%;"} Put the data in a list and generate random initial values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jd.lm <- list(x=width, y=mass, n=length(mass)) # Data ji.lm <- function() list(beta0=rnorm(1), beta1=0, sigmaSq=runif(1)) # Initial values jp.lm <- c("beta0", "beta1", "sigmaSq") # Parameters ``` ::: ## Bayesian linear regression -- inference {style="font-size: 90%;"} Use MCMC to draw posterior samples: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(jagsUI) js.lm <- jags.basic(data=jd.lm, inits=ji.lm, parameters.to.save=jp.lm, model.file="lm.jag", n.chains=1, n.iter=1000) ``` :::
::: {.fragment} Summarize the posterior samples: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(summary(js.lm)$quant, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% beta0 -0.52 -0.15 0.04 0.21 0.63 beta1 -0.32 0.27 0.52 0.80 1.32 deviance -2.58 -0.97 0.95 3.41 9.35 sigmaSq 0.03 0.05 0.08 0.12 0.26 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Bayesian linear regression -- inference {style="font-size: 90%;"} View the posterior samples ::: {.cell layout-align="center" fig-heigth='12'} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(js.lm[,1:2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/lm-jags-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=7in} ::: ::: ## Linear models A more general depiction of linear models: $$ \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} \\ y_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma^2) $$ where the $\beta$'s are coefficients, and the $x$ values are predictor variables (or dummy variables for categorical predictors). ## Interpreting the $\beta$ coefficients You need to be able to interpret the $\beta$ coefficients for *any model* that you fit to your data.
A linear model might have dozens of continuous and categorical predictors variables, with dozens of associated $\beta$ coefficients.
Linear models can also include polynomial terms and interactions. ## Interpreting the $\beta$'s The intercept ($\beta_0$) is the expected value of $y$, when all $x=0$.\ . . .
If $x_1$ is a **continuous** explanatory variable: - $\beta_1$ can usually be interpreted as a *slope* parameter. - In this case, $\beta_1$ is the change in $y$ resulting from a 1 unit change in $x_1$ (while holding the other predictors constant). ## Interpreting $\beta$'s for categorical explanatory variables {style="font-size: 90%;"} Things are more complicated for **categorical** explanatory variables (i.e., factors) because they must be converted to dummy variables. There are many ways of creating dummy variables. In `R`, the default method for creating dummy variables from unordered factors works like this: - One level of the factor is treated as a [reference level]{.alert}. - The reference level is associated with the intercept. - The $\beta$ coefficients for the other levels of the factor are differences from the reference level. ## Interpreting $\beta$'s for categorical explanatory variables {style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lm(mass~species) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = mass ~ species) Coefficients: (Intercept) species2 species3 species4 10.2147 0.9994 -1.3335 0.6294 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/mass-species-bar-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Ruffed grouse ![](figs/RUGR.jpg){width="80%" fig-align="center"} ## Ruffed grouse survey design ![](figs/grouse_map_locs.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"} ## Grouse data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grouse.data <- read.csv("grouse_data_glm.csv", row.names=1) grouse.data$route <- factor(grouse.data$route) grouse.data$utmZone <- factor(grouse.data$utmZone) head(grouse.data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` abundance presence route utmE utmN utmZone elevation 101_1 0 0 101 760582 3873068 16S 574.68 101_10 0 0 101 760582 3873068 16S 574.68 101_2 0 0 101 760582 3873068 16S 574.68 101_3 0 0 101 760582 3873068 16S 574.68 101_4 0 0 101 760582 3873068 16S 574.68 101_5 0 0 101 760582 3873068 16S 574.68 ``` ::: ::: ## Grouse regression ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fm1 <- lm(abundance ~ elevation, grouse.data) summary(fm1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = abundance ~ elevation, data = grouse.data) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -0.04734 -0.03984 -0.03718 -0.02733 1.96076 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 6.415e-02 3.329e-02 1.927 0.0545 . elevation -4.327e-05 4.697e-05 -0.921 0.3573 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.2093 on 577 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.001469, Adjusted R-squared: -0.0002616 F-statistic: 0.8488 on 1 and 577 DF, p-value: 0.3573 ``` ::: ::: ## Grouse prediction {style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,3,4,5|6|7,8"} elev.min <- min(grouse.data$elevation) elev.max <- max(grouse.data$elevation) seq.length <- 20 ## Determines how smooth the function looks in GLMs elev.seq <- seq(from=elev.min, to=elev.max, length.out=seq.length) pred.data <- data.frame(elevation=elev.seq) pred.elev <- predict(fm1, newdata=pred.data, se=TRUE) plot(abundance ~ elevation, data=grouse.data, ylim=c(0,2)) lines(elev.seq, pred.elev$fit, col="blue", lwd=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=4in} ::: ::: # Generalized linear models {visibility="hidden"} ## Generalized linear models (GLMs) {style="font-size: 90%;"}
The residuals don't have to be normally distributed.
The response variable can be binary, integer, strictly-positive, etc\...
The variance is not assumed to be constant.
Useful for manipulative experiments or observational studies, just like linear models. ## From linear to generalized linear {style="font-size: 90%;"} Linear model $$ \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} \\ y_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma^2) $$ . . . Generalized Linear model $$ g(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} \\ y_i \sim f(\mu_i) $$ where\ $g$ is a link function, such as the log or logit link\ $f$ is a probability distribution such as the binomial or Poisson ## Link functions {style="font-size: 90%;"} An inverse link function ($g^{-1}$) transforms values from the $(-\infty,\infty)$ scale to the scale of interest, such as $(0,1)$ for probabilities. The link function ($g$) does the reverse.
Distribution link name link equation inverse link equation -------------- --------------- ----------------------- ----------------------------- Binomial logit $\log(\frac{p}{1-p})$ $\frac{\mu}{1 + \exp(\mu)}$ Poisson log $\log(\lambda)$ $\exp(\mu)$ ## Link functions in R Distribution link name link in **R** inv link in **R** -------------- ----------- --------------- ------------------- Binomial logit `qlogis` `plogis` Poisson log `log` `exp` ## Logit link example ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(function(x) 5 + -0.08*x, from=0, to=100, xlab="Elevation", ylab="logit(prob of occurrence)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/nologit-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ## Logit link example ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(function(x) plogis(5 + -0.08*x), from=0, to=100, xlab="Elevation", ylab="Probability of occurrence") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/logit-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: # Logistic regression ## Logistic Regression {style="font-size: 80%;"} Logistic regression is a specific type of GLM in which the response variable follows a binomial distribution and the link function is the logit. . . .
It would be better to call it "binomial regression" since other link functions (e.g. the probit) can be used. . . .
Appropriate when the response is binary or a count with an upper limit Examples: - Presence/absence studies - Survival studies - Disease prevalence studies ## Logistic Regression $$ \mathrm{logit}(p_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots \\ y_i \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N, p_i) $$
where:\ $N$ is the number of "trials" (e.g. coin flips)\ $p_i$ is the probability of success for sample unit $i$ ## Binomial distribution -- fair coin {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/fair-coin-1.png){fig-align='center' width=6in} ::: ::: ## Binomial distribution -- warped coin {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/warped-coin-1.png){fig-align='center' width=6in} ::: ::: ## Binomial distribution Properties - The expected value of $y$ is $Np$ - The variance is $Np(1-p)$ . . . Bernoulli distribution - The Bernoulli distribution is a binomial distribution with a single trial ($N=1$) - Logistic regression is usually done in this context, such that the response variable is 0/1 or No/Yes or Bad/Good, etc$\dots$ ## Logistic regression example 1. How could we fit the following model to the grouse data? $$ \begin{gathered} \mathrm{logit}(p_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathrm{ELEV}_i \\ y_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(p_i) \end{gathered} $$ 2. How can we predict and graph occurrence probability ($p$) over a range of elevations? ## Logistic regression example {.smaller} Fit the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} logitreg1 <- glm(presence ~ elevation, data=grouse.data, family=binomial(link="logit")) logitreg1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = presence ~ elevation, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = grouse.data) Coefficients: (Intercept) elevation -3.0451857 -0.0006727 Degrees of Freedom: 578 Total (i.e. Null); 577 Residual Null Deviance: 153.5 Residual Deviance: 153.2 AIC: 157.2 ``` ::: ::: . . .
Predict ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} elev.min <- min(grouse.data$elevation) elev.max <- max(grouse.data$elevation) seq.length <- 20 ## Determines how smooth the function looks in GLMs elev.seq <- seq(from=elev.min, to=elev.max, length.out=seq.length) pred.data.lr <- data.frame(elevation=elev.seq) pred.elev <- predict(logitreg1, newdata=pred.data.lr, type="link", se=TRUE) ``` ::: ## Logistic regression example {.smaller} Predictions and standard errors. Notice that we predict on the link scale, and then back-transform after adding the SE. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(presence ~ elevation, data=grouse.data, ylim=c(0,1), xlab="Elevation", ylab="Presence", cex.lab=1.3) lines(elev.seq, plogis(pred.elev$fit), col="blue", lwd=2) lines(elev.seq, plogis(pred.elev$fit+pred.elev$se.fit), col="blue", lwd=1, lty=2) lines(elev.seq, plogis(pred.elev$fit-pred.elev$se.fit), col="blue", lwd=1, lty=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=4.5in} ::: ::: # Poisson regression ## Poisson Regression $$ \mathrm{log}(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} \\ y_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i) $$ where:\ $\lambda_i$ is the expected value of $y_i$\ ## Poisson regression {style="font-size: 80%;"} Useful for: - Count data - Number of events in time intervals - Other types of integer data . . .
Properties - The expected value of $y$ ($\lambda$) is equal to the variance - This is an assumption of the Poisson model - Like all assumptions, it can be relaxed if you have enough data ## Poisson distribution ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/pois-1.png){fig-align="center" width="5.5in"} ## Poisson distribution ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/pois-2.png){fig-align="center" width="5.5in"} ## Poisson distribution ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/pois-3.png){fig-align="center" width="5.5in"} ## Log link example ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(function(x) 5 + -0.08*x, from=0, to=100, xlab="Elevation", ylab="log(Expected abundance)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/nolog-link-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ## Log link example ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(function(x) exp(5 + -0.08*x), from=0, to=100, xlab="Elevation", ylab="Expected abundance") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/log-link-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ## Poisson regression simulation {style="font-size: 70%;"} First, create a covariate: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 100 x <- rnorm(n) ``` ::: . . . Next, pick values for the coefficients and compute $\lambda_i = E(y_i)$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beta0 <- -1 beta1 <- 1 lam <- exp(beta0 + beta1*x) ``` ::: . . . Now, simulate the response variable $y$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- rpois(n=n, lambda=lam) ``` ::: . . . Finally, fit the model: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (poisreg1 <- glm(y ~ x, family=poisson(link="log"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = y ~ x, family = poisson(link = "log")) Coefficients: (Intercept) x -1.080 1.172 Degrees of Freedom: 99 Total (i.e. Null); 98 Residual Null Deviance: 307.4 Residual Deviance: 87.7 AIC: 179.6 ``` ::: ::: ## Bayesian Poisson regression {style="font-size: 80%;"} The model is in a text file named `glm.jag` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model { # Priors beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1) ## Normal prior with mean=0, variance=10 beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1) ## Model for the data for(i in 1:n) { lambda[i] <- exp(beta0 + beta1*x[i]) y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i]) } } ``` ::: . . .
Put the data in a list and pick some initial values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jd.glm <- list(x=x, y=y, n=length(y)) ji.glm <- function() list(beta0=rnorm(1), beta1=rnorm(1)) jp.glm <- c("beta0", "beta1") ``` ::: ## Bayesian Poisson regression Use MCMC to draw posterior samples: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(jagsUI) js.glm <- jags.basic(data=jd.glm, inits=ji.glm, parameters.to.save=jp.glm, model.file="glm.jag", n.chains=2, n.iter=1000) ``` :::
::: {.fragment} Summarize the posterior samples: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(summary(js.glm)$quant, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% beta0 -1.51 -1.22 -1.04 -0.91 -0.58 beta1 0.96 1.10 1.16 1.23 1.33 deviance 175.66 176.38 177.34 178.88 187.97 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Bayesian Poisson regression -- inference {style="font-size: 90%;"} View the posterior samples ::: {.cell layout-align="center" fig-heigth='12'} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(js.glm[,1:2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stats-basics_files/figure-revealjs/glm-jags-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=7in} ::: ::: ## Assignment {.smaller} Create a self-contained R script (or better yet an Rmarkdown file) to do the following: 1. Simulate logistic regression data according to $y_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(p_i)$ and $\mathrm{logit}(p_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$ with $\beta_0=-1$ and $\beta_1=1$. Generate the covariate using [`x <- rnorm(n=100)`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"}. Note that you will need to use the [`rbinom`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} function to simulate Bernoulli outcomes. 2. Fit a logistic regression model to the simulated data ($y$ and $x$) using the [`glm`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} function. Create a figure showing $x$ and $y$ with the fitted regression line. Use [`predict`]{style="background-color: inlinecolor"} to get the fitted line. 3. Fit the logistic regression model in JAGS. Use $\mathrm{Normal}(0, var=10)$ priors for the regression coefficients. 4. Compare and intepret the estimates of $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ from the classical analysis and the Bayesian analysis. Upload your `.R` or `.Rmd` or `.qmd` file to ELC by 5:00 PM Tuesday.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
